\begin{frame}{The problem}
  Cognitive theories are stated in prose, in simulation code, or as equations fitted to data.
  \bigskip
  \begin{itemize}
    \item What follows from a theory's \emph{core assumptions}, as distinct from its parameter settings or implementation details, is rarely checked.
    \item A simulation shows that a model \emph{can} produce a result, with these parameters and these stimuli.
    \item It doesn't show which assumptions produced it, whether it survives other parameters, or whether a rival theory would produce it just as well.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 1, why: what simulation leaves open.
\begin{itemize}
\item Most modelling evidence is a fit: one model, one set of parameters, compared with data.
\item That's valuable, but it leaves three questions open: which assumptions did the work, is the result robust, and does it discriminate between theories?
\item The rest of the talk is about answering those questions with proofs.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Three kinds of evidence a theory can give}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{p{0.3\linewidth}p{0.3\linewidth}p{0.3\linewidth}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{One run} & \textbf{Every run} & \textbf{Every model satisfying the postulates}\\
    \midrule
    one model, one parameter setting & one model, all its executions & all models the theory allows\\
    the theory \emph{can} do it & that model \emph{always} does it & the postulates \emph{entail} it\\
    simulation & model checking, sweeps & proof\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \bigskip

  CogLean is built around the third kind, and keeps the other two in the same language.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item A theorem quantified over every model satisfying the postulates says which assumptions matter (the proof uses some and not others), what is robust, and whether a claim is possibility or necessity.
\item Simulation is still essential: it explores, suggests conjectures, and fits data. Proof settles which conjectures follow from which assumptions. Experiments with people decide whether the assumptions are right.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Why Lean}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{One definition, run and proved.} The same definition of a memory can be \emph{run} on an experiment's stimuli and \emph{proved about} for all stimuli. The simulation and the theory can't drift apart.
    \item \textbf{Checked.} Every proof step is checked by a small trusted kernel.
    \item \textbf{General.} A theorem can quantify over all nets, all parameter values, all stimulus lists.
    \item \textbf{Cumulative.} Like Mathlib for mathematics: definitions made once, theorems imported rather than re-derived.
  \end{itemize}
  \bigskip
  \textit{The guarantee is relative.} Lean checks that a theorem follows from the definitions, not that the definitions capture the theory, still less that the theory is true of people.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Mathlib is a single, shared, machine-checked library of mathematics. CogLean aims at the same thing for cognitive theory.
\item The caveat on this slide matters and will come back: proofs are only as faithful as the formal definitions.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Two theories, combined}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \column{0.5\textwidth}
    \textbf{EPAM} (Feigenbaum 1959)
    \begin{itemize}\small
      \item Stimuli are feature codes.
      \item A discrimination net sorts a code by testing features, down to a stored image.
      \item Learning grows a test only where two codes are confused, on the first difference noticed.
      \item So an unfamiliar code that agrees on every tested feature is \emph{recognized as} a familiar one.
    \end{itemize}
    \column{0.5\textwidth}
    \textbf{Distributions of associations} (Siegler \& Shrager 1984)
    \begin{itemize}\small
      \item Each problem has associations to answers, with strengths.
      \item Sample an answer in proportion to strength; state it if it clears a confidence criterion; try up to $n$ times.
      \item Otherwise, use a backup strategy.
      \item Retrieval is used with probability $1-(1-R)^n$.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 2, a theory proved: two classic models combined into one of multi-digit addition.
\begin{itemize}
\item $R$ is the chance that one search clears the criterion. Both theories' phenomena are already proved in the library.
\item In DOA, a flat distribution raises both errors and backup use; they go together. That fact is what the next slides break.
\end{itemize}
}

    \draw[arr] (p) -- (r); \draw[arr] (r) -- (s); \draw[arr] (s) -- (a);
    \draw[arr] (r) |- node[pos=0.25, left]{\scriptsize not recognized} (b);
    \draw[arr] (s) -- node[right]{\scriptsize exhausted} (b);
    \draw[arr] (b) -| (a);
  \end{tikzpicture}
  \end{center}
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item Every postulate is a parameter: the encoding, the net, the strengths, the criterion, the search length, the backup.
    \item 18 predictions, each proved for every choice of them.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The column backup is built from single-digit DOA trials chained by carries. Carrying adds no error: a column error is a single-digit error moved to its place.
\item The predictions include near misses (within 200 or 20, depending on which digits the net tests), harmless confusions (same sum, commuted problems), and no interference with practiced problems.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Confident errors}
  Let a familiar problem $q$ have \emph{sharp} associations (only its correct sum clears the criterion), and let $x$, with a different sum, be recognized as $q$. Then:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item on $q$, whole-problem retrieval never errs;
    \item on $x$, every whole-problem answer is wrong;
    \item $x$ uses the backup exactly as rarely as $q$ does: $(1-R_q)^n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  \bigskip
  In DOA alone, errors and backup use rise together. Confusion breaks the tie: a retrieved, wrong answer with no extra backup use.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item This is the prediction neither theory makes alone.
\item Two cautions. The model has no timing, so ``fast'' would need a timing model. And the errors are frequent only if retrieval on $q$ usually succeeds ($R_q$ near 1); if $R_q = 0$, every trial uses the backup.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{A worked case}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Encoding: each digit in four bits (24 features). The net learns $100+100$ and $100+200$, which differ only in the second addend's hundreds digit, so that is all it tests.
    \item Associations: $.90$ on each problem's sum, $.01$ elsewhere; criterion $.50$; search length 1.
    \item $150+100$ is recognized as $100+100$.
  \end{itemize}
  \bigskip
  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lc}
    \toprule
    $150+100$ answered $200$, by retrieval & $45/46$\\
    $150+100$ answered $250$, by the columns & $1/46$\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item These numbers are for illustration, computed exactly by the Lean kernel. The structural result, confident errors, holds for every parameter choice.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{In words: Confident errors: the proof is a composition}
  \textbf{Theorem (confident errors).} Suppose:
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item a familiar problem $q$ calls up its own code for certain, and a stranger $x$ calls up $q$'s code for certain;
    \item $q$'s associations are \emph{sharp}: only $q$'s correct answer clears the criterion;
    \item $x$'s correct answer is different; no association set has total strength 0; the backups are proper distributions.
  \end{itemize}
  Then (1) $q$ is never given a wrong whole answer; (2) every whole answer given to $x$ is wrong; (3) $x$ and $q$ use the backup equally often.
  \medskip

  \textbf{Proof.}
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item (1) is the next lemma, applied to $q$ itself.
    \item (2): on sharp associations every stated answer is $q$'s correct answer, which is wrong for $x$.
    \item (3): both problems search the same associations, so each uses the backup with probability $(1-R_q)^n$.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 3, how: the proof in words, then the actual Lean.
}

\begin{frame}[fragile]{Confident errors: the proof is a composition}
\begin{Verbatim}
theorem confident_errors (correct : P → A) (x q : P) (hT : ∀ y, total as (str y) ≠ 0)
    (hbx : mass (backup x) = 1) (hbq : mass (backup q) = 1)
    (hq : retrieve (code q) = pure (some (code q)))
    (hx : retrieve (code x) = pure (some (code q)))
    (hs : Sharp str cc (code q) (correct q)) (hne : correct x ≠ correct q) :
    prob (recognizeRetrieve code retrieve str as cc n backup q) (wholeWrong correct q) = 0 ∧
      prob (recognizeRetrieve code retrieve str as cc n backup x) (wholeWrong correct x) =
        prob (recognizeRetrieve code retrieve str as cc n backup x) isWhole ∧
      prob (recognizeRetrieve code retrieve str as cc n backup x) isBackup =
        prob (recognizeRetrieve code retrieve str as cc n backup q) isBackup := by
  refine ⟨confusion_gives_neighbours_answer code retrieve str as cc n backup correct q q (hT _) hq hs,
    wrong_eq_whole_of_sharp code retrieve str as cc n backup correct x _ _ (hT _) hx hs hne, ?_⟩
  rw [backup_prob_certain code retrieve str as cc n backup x _ hx hbx hT,
    backup_prob_certain code retrieve str as cc n backup q _ hq hbq hT]
\end{Verbatim}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Three conjuncts, three earlier lemmas. The first is the neighbour's-answer lemma applied to $q$ itself; the second says that on sharp associations, every stated answer to $x$ is wrong; the third rewrites both backup probabilities to the same closed form $(1-R_q)^n$, after which the goal is an identity.
\item Note the hypotheses: retrieval is certain (\code{= pure (some \ldots)}). That is exactly what ACT-R never satisfies, and what the laws later supply.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}[fragile]{What is checked, and what is not}
\begin{Verbatim}
#print axioms Cog.RR.confident_errors_of_laws
'Cog.RR.confident_errors_of_laws' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
\end{Verbatim}
  \medskip
  \begin{itemize}
    \item No \code{sorry} anywhere; only Lean's three standard axioms.
    \item Core Lean only: no Mathlib, so everything computes.
    \item \textbf{Not checked}: that the definitions say what EPAM, DOA or ACT-R say. That is what the prose specification, the blind simulation, and (planned) comparison with PyACTUp are for.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The three axioms are those every Lean development uses: propositional extensionality, choice, and quotient soundness.
\item Code: \code{CogLib/CogLib/Rep/Distribution.lean}, \code{Memory/DiscriminationNet.lean}, \code{Process/SampledRetrieval.lean}, \code{Process/RecognizeRetrieve.lean}, \code{Phenomena/RetrievalLaws.lean}; \code{MultiDigit/MultiDigit/AnyMemory.lean}; \code{Experiments/Experiments/FaceNaming.lean}.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The idea: two independent readings}
  \centering
  \begin{tikzpicture}
    \node[box] (spec) at (0,0) {prose\\specification};
    \node[box] (lean) at (3.8,1) {Lean\\formalization};
    \node[box] (py) at (3.8,-1) {blind Python\\simulator};
    \node[box] (pred) at (7.6,1) {theorems $\to$\\preregistered checks};
    \node[box] (logs) at (7.6,-1) {simulated\\trials};
    \node[box] (cmp) at (11,0) {compare};
    \draw[arr] (spec) -- (lean); \draw[arr] (spec) -- (py);
    \draw[arr] (lean) -- (pred); \draw[arr] (py) -- (logs);
    \draw[arr] (pred) -- (cmp); \draw[arr] (logs) -- (cmp);
  \end{tikzpicture}
  \bigskip
  \raggedright

  N-version programming (Avi\v{z}ienis 1985), applied to a theory. A disagreement means one of three things: the prose is ambiguous, the formalization drifted, or the simulator has a bug.
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 4, is it faithful: a blind simulation against preregistered predictions.
\begin{itemize}
\item In fault-tolerant software, several teams implement one specification independently, and their disagreements locate the faults. Here the two versions are the Lean formalization and a simulator written without seeing it.
\item The Lean side also exports exact outcome distributions for shared instances, so some comparisons are exact, not just statistical.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The procedure}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A prose specification} (\code{SPEC.md}): the model in plain words, with no Lean names, theorems, or predictions. Points the prose leaves open are listed as \emph{open choices}.
    \item \textbf{A preregistration} (\code{PREREG.md}): each theorem's observable statistic and how it is judged. Committed \emph{before} the simulator existed; the implementer never saw it.
    \item \textbf{A blind implementer}: a fresh AI agent, given only the specification, in an empty directory. Its tool calls were audited: it read only files it had written.
    \item \textbf{Lean's exact distributions} for four shared instances.
    \item \textbf{A harness} (\code{compare.py}): random instances, the preregistered checks, and a report.
  \end{enumerate}
  \medskip
  \small Commits, 26 October 2026: specification and preregistration 19:16; simulator, unmodified, 19:21; harness and results 19:31.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The commit timestamps are the preregistration's evidence: the checks were fixed before any simulator output existed.
\item The simulator is committed exactly as delivered. Disagreements are recorded, not fixed in place.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Finding 1: five predictions were never tested}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Predictions 6a, 6b, 14, 17 and 18 need the net's path to test \emph{every} feature of a digit or a column: 4 bits, 9 thresholds, or 100 fact features.
    \item EPAM grows one test per confusion, so paths are short. In no learned net did the hypothesis ever hold.
    \item The theorems are true. But they say almost nothing about the nets EPAM actually learns.
  \end{itemize}
  \bigskip
  \textit{Lesson.} A theorem can be correct and nearly irrelevant to the models the theory produces. Restate it in terms of what learned nets do test: for example, ``the tested bits of a digit restrict it to a set''.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Without the non-vacuity rule, these would have been reported as five passes.
\item This is a finding about proving things in cognitive science generally: hypotheses that make a proof go through can quietly exclude the cases of interest.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Finding 3: a prediction depends on an open choice}
  The predicted learning sequence: a confident error, then column work, then fluent correct retrieval.
  \medskip
  \small
  \begin{center}
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
  \begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
    \toprule
    O2: new problem starts with & discriminated & canonical & settles on correct & mixed & trapped on error\\
    \midrule
    no associations & 48 & 40 & 7 & 1 & 0\\
    only the correct answer & 61 & 28 & 33 & 0 & 0\\
    a copy of the neighbour's & 44 & 0 & 2 & 35 & 7\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}}
  \end{center}
  \medskip
  \normalsize
  \begin{itemize}
    \item With no associations, the predicted sequence appears (40 of 48).
    \item Starting with the correct answer, the column phase is often skipped.
    \item Copying the neighbour's associations perpetuates the error.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item This part was exploratory, not preregistered: learning over many trials is not yet proved in Lean.
\item The model leaves O2 open, and the prediction depends on it. Which reading is right is a substantive question about the theory, now sharply posed.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The generality problem}
  There are a great many specific models: EPAM, ACT-R, SAM, REM, MINERVA~2, TODAM, connectionist networks\ldots
  \bigskip
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Formalizing them one at a time doesn't scale.
    \item A pile of formalized models doesn't say what any two of them \emph{disagree} about.
    \item And none of them is ``true'': unlike mathematics, there's no settled foundation to build on.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 5, generalizing: memory as a plug-in, and a composition reused across tasks.
\begin{itemize}
\item This is the central design question. The answer on the next slides is to organize the library around laws, the way Mathlib organizes algebra.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Six laws}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.74\linewidth}}
    \toprule
    Certainty & An item just studied is retrieved by itself with probability 1.\\
    Stability & Studying $z$ leaves the chance that $y$ retrieves itself unchanged.\\
    Order-freedom & Swapping the last two study events leaves retrieval unchanged, for every probe.\\
    Recency & Of two new items studied last, a probe equally similar to both retrieves the later more often.\\
    Stored-only & Nothing is retrieved that was never studied.\\
    Determinacy & Every retrieval has a single outcome.\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 6, laws: compare families of models by the laws they have.
\begin{itemize}
\item Order-freedom is deliberately narrow: only the last two events are swapped, and only retrieval must agree, not the memory state.
\item Determinacy is structural as stated, but each ``lacks'' cell exhibits two outcomes with positive probability, so it fails any probabilistic version too.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Four families}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Discrimination} (EPAM): a net of feature tests; learning grows a test where codes are confused.
    \item \textbf{Activation} (ACT-R declarative memory): each use adds activation that decays; partial matching; a failure weight. Decay 1, temperature 1: exactly rational.
    \item \textbf{Strength with a criterion} (after DOA): strengths only add; sample by strength, discounted by mismatch; state if above criterion.
    \item \textbf{Global matching} (MINERVA~2): every study stores a trace; a probe activates all traces by the cube of similarity; memory returns the \emph{echo}, their weighted blend.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Each family is formalized once, with its parameters free. A published model is a choice of parameters within its family.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The matrix}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
    \toprule
    & Certainty & Stability & Order-free & Recency & Stored-only & Determinate\\
    \midrule
    Discrimination & \has & \has & \lacks & \lacks & \has & \has\\
    Activation & \lacks & \lacks & \lacks & \has & \has & \lacks\\
    Strength & \lacks & \lacks & \has & \lacks & \has & \lacks\\
    Global matching & \lacks & \lacks & \has & \lacks & \lacks & \has\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \bigskip
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \has: a general proof, for every parameter choice meeting stated conditions.
    \item \lacks: a counterexample, computed exactly on the eight 3-bit codes.
    \item Every law is had by some family and lacked by another; every family has its own row. A script checks both.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Examples of ``has'': EPAM's certainty needs only that the items be noticeably different; ACT-R's recency holds for any positive mismatch discount and failure weight (the later item is retrieved exactly twice as often); strength memory and MINERVA are order-free for every parameter choice.
\item A ``lacks'' cell says only that the law fails somewhere. Mapping the parameter regions where a family does have it is open.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The laws were tested, and failed once}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item The first four laws were chosen with three families in view.
    \item Global matching was added as a test. On those four laws, it had \emph{exactly} the row of strength memory.
    \item So the laws missed something. What is distinctive about global matching? Its output is a blend.
    \item Study $110$, $101$, $011$; probe with $111$ (their prototype, never studied): MINERVA returns $111$.
    \item Hence the stored-only law, which separates them.
  \end{itemize}
  \bigskip
  Rule: a law enters only with a witness on each side.
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item A law every family satisfies, or satisfies only vacuously, tells theories apart by accident. An earlier all-or-none law, ``stable retrieval'', turned out to hold for ACT-R only vacuously, because nothing in ACT-R is retrieved for certain; that is now a theorem.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{From laws: which memories give confident errors?}
  \textbf{Theorem.} Any memory with three laws (\emph{determinacy}, \emph{certainty}, \emph{stability}) produces confident errors whenever a stranger can be taken for a studied item with sharp associations.
  \bigskip
  \begin{itemize}
    \item In the matrix of memory families, only discrimination (EPAM) has all three.
    \item Face naming's confident misnaming is derived this way, from EPAM's matrix cells plus one computed fact (Carl can be taken for Bob).
    \item The evidence judges that people lack certainty. So explaining confident errors in people needs a graded version: these laws with high probability, not probability 1.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item This is where the composition and the law matrix meet: the matrix now says which families produce the phenomenon.
\item The graded theorem is open.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Reversing the workflow}
  Usually: choose an experiment, compute each theory's predictions.
  \bigskip

  Instead:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item find two laws that disagree;
    \item derive a design on which they make incompatible predictions;
    \item prove the separation, for every memory with either law;
    \item state the response model that connects it to what participants say.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 7, experiments from laws: start from a disagreement, derive the design, prove the separation.
\begin{itemize}
\item This makes the matrix an experiment generator rather than a scoreboard.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Recency against order-freedom}
  \textbf{Design.} Two new items $a$, $b$; a probe $x$ equally similar to both.
  Condition AB studies $a$ then $b$; condition BA studies $b$ then $a$; both probe with $x$.
  \[
  D = P(\text{retrieve } b) - P(\text{retrieve } a), \qquad \Delta = D_{AB} - D_{BA}.
  \]
  \textbf{Theorems}, for any memory:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item order-freedom $\Rightarrow \Delta = 0$;
    \item recency $\Rightarrow \Delta > 0$;
    \item so no memory has both laws, wherever such a design exists.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Recency applied to $(a, b)$ gives $D_{AB} > 0$; applied to $(b, a)$ it gives $D_{BA} < 0$. Order-freedom makes the two conditions' retrieval identical.
\item These proofs never mention EPAM, ACT-R, or any parameter.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{From retrieval to report}
  \textbf{Forced choice}: report A if $a$ is retrieved, B if $b$ is; otherwise guess B with probability $\gamma$.
  \[
  \Delta_{\text{report}} = \Delta + (2\gamma - 1)\,(o_{AB} - o_{BA}),
  \]
  where $o$ is the chance of retrieving neither item.
  \bigskip
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Order-freedom: $\Delta_{\text{report}} = 0$, for every $\gamma$.
    \item Recency: $\Delta_{\text{report}} > 0$ with unbiased guessing, or when ``neither'' is equally likely in both orders.
    \item A biased guesser can mask or reverse the recency prediction.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The bridge carries its own condition, stated in the theorem: laws plus a response model give an observable contrast.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{The same design, four memories}
  \small
  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lccl}
    \toprule
    Memory & $\Delta$, no prior item & $\Delta$, after 000 & why\\
    \midrule
    ACT-R & $10/17$ & & recency, so $\Delta > 0$\\
    Strength & $0$ & $0$ & order-free\\
    MINERVA & $0$ & $0$ & order-free\\
    EPAM & $0$ & $-2$ & neither law: computed\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \bigskip
  \normalsize
  \begin{itemize}
    \item ACT-R's reported effect is $10/17$ for every guessing bias: both orders leave the same chance of ``neither''.
    \item EPAM shows the most extreme \emph{primacy} possible. After 000, whichever item is learned first is discriminated from it, and the probe always retrieves that one. Its order effects come from the shape of the net, not from time.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item One counterbalanced experiment gives recency, no effect, or primacy, depending on the family, and the matrix says in advance which.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{What is true here?}
  In mathematics, a proved theorem is true. Here there are only competing theories. What can a library build on?
  \bigskip
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{p{0.32\linewidth}p{0.36\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}}
    \toprule
    Claim & Example & Status\\
    \midrule
    A law entails a prediction & stability $\Rightarrow$ practiced items stay practiced & proved, permanent\\
    A family has a law & discrimination nets have stability & proved, permanent\\
    People have a law & people lack stability in recall & empirical, revisable\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \bigskip

  \normalsize
  Which theory is right follows from the second and third rows together.
\end{frame}
\note{
\textbf{Transition.} Part 8, what is true: conditional results, evidence, and limits.
\begin{itemize}
\item The conditional results don't expire. They stay true even if every family in the library is refuted.
\item Mathlib is in the same position more often than it seems: it proves facts about Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry alike, and leaves to physics which one space is.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Against the evidence}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
    \toprule
    & Certainty & Stability & Order-free & Recency & Stored-only & Determinate\\
    \midrule
    People (judged) & \emph{lacks} & \emph{mixed} & \emph{lacks} & \emph{has} & \emph{mixed} & \emph{mixed}\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \bigskip
  \normalsize
  \begin{itemize}
    \item A judgment, not a theorem, with sources, kept apart from the proofs.
    \item Each entry states its \textbf{bridge}: how a measure (a report) is taken to show a law (about retrieval).
    \item Activation fits every settled entry, but each fit rests on unformalized bridges.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Sources: Tulving \& Pearlstone 1966 (certainty); McGeoch 1932, Barnes \& Underwood 1959, Ratcliff, Clark \& Shiffrin 1990 (stability: interference in recall, no list-strength effect in recognition); Murdock 1962 and Glanzer \& Cunitz 1966 (order, recency); Posner \& Keele 1968 and Roediger \& McDermott 1995 (stored-only).
\item Stored-only is mixed because endorsing a prototype as old doesn't show the prototype was retrieved; next slide.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Where this is weaker than mathematics}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Definitions are contestable.} A family is one formalization of a theory. We check that link with blind simulations and community implementations.
    \item \textbf{Laws are idealizations} and presuppose a representation (binary codes, feature-count similarity).
    \item \textbf{Families are flexible.} The informative facts are parameter regions, not single counterexamples.
    \item \textbf{Evidence is never final.} The empirical row will change; the proved rows won't, and the matrix says at once what follows.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The blind simulation: a fresh agent wrote a Python simulator from a prose specification alone, against predictions preregistered before it existed. It agreed with Lean's exact distributions on every test, and exposed gaps in the formalization.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Next}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Learning across trials}: feedback updates memory, so memory states become random; multi-digit learning sequences are the target.
    \item \textbf{Graded laws}, and the parameter regions of the ``lacks'' cells.
    \item \textbf{More families as tests}: REM, a connectionist memory, CHREST, ACT-R with blending.
    \item \textbf{Observational semantics}: decision and report components, so laws about retrieval predict what participants say.
    \item \textbf{Beyond memory}: strategy choice, then production systems.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item The Common Model of Cognition is a useful checklist for which interfaces to add, not a foundation to impose.
\end{itemize}
}

\begin{frame}{Take-home}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Cognitive theories can be stated so that their consequences are \emph{proved}, for every parameter setting.
    \item The durable content is conditional: laws entail predictions; families have or lack laws.
    \item A matrix of families against laws tells you which experiments are worth running, and what a result refutes.
    \item The value is not just that EPAM, ACT-R and others can each be formalized, but that results about one component can be combined with results about another to give predictions none of them anticipated.
  \end{itemize}
  \bigskip
  \centering\small github.com/jeffshrager/CogLean
\end{frame}
\note{
\begin{itemize}
\item Two detailed talks follow up: one on recognition, retrieval and confident errors; one on the laws, the matrix and experiments derived from laws.
\end{itemize}
}
